newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania university ransacked by rioters.
newsitem.headline: Albania university ransacked by rioters.

text.p: Downcast professors and staff on Tuesday cleared away charred books, smashed equipment and piles of glass and rubble left by two days of frenzied rioting last week by armed men at Albania's Agricultural University.

Rows of books in the library, reputed by staff to contain some of the finest scientific reference materials in the country, were reduced to mounds of ash at the campus, about nine km (six miles) outside the capital.
Parts from photocopiers lay strewn among ankle-deep piles of journals, photographs and long strings of film negatives.
Two women technicians poured a soapy mixture on to the floor to remove an unctuous black mass -- a noxious cocktail, they said, of ammonia, acids and plant hormones from smashed containers.
"Is this the outcome of our new democracy? This is an unspeakable crime!" said chief librarian Floresha Nasho, wincing as she surveyed gutted stacks.
"I've been here for 17 years. We worked hard to develop new technology. I never saw such things even in 1990 when we got rid of communism. Only a single room of books was saved."

Staff said hundreds of men carrying rifles and pistols descended on the campus on Thursday evening, when Tirana was on the brink of total lawlessness after gangs looted army depots throughout most of the Balkan country.
With police and the army all but abandoning their posts, the men tore through offices and classrooms again on Friday before some order was restored to the capital in the evening.
The rioters tore out tiling, aluminium doors, panes of glass, wall outlets -- everything that could be used in homes -- and smashed whatever else came to hand.
Dozens of computers were taken away. One student said some rioters believed computer terminals were television sets.
"I ran in here and they were overturning an instrument measuring light intensity and a sterile chamber," said technician Flora Marku, tears welling up in her eyes.
"I screamed at them to leave the equipment alone. It was of no use to them. They just told me to get out of the way."
The owner of the main campus cafe, adjacent to the gutted library, said he kept the rioters out by standing his ground at the entrance, a Kalashnikov rifle slung over his shoulder.
"They were crazed, furious," he said. "You could hardly say this was human behaviour."
The university had been a showcase of cooperation with Western academics six years after the fall of eastern Europe's most repressive and isolationist communist regime.
German and U.S. academics taught there and professors said the equivalent of $4 million in grants had come from Germany alone.

Staff said they believed the mayhem was caused by natives of poorer northern Albania who had been living in tumbledown shacks opposite the campus since coming to Tirana in the early 1990s in search of work.
Students alleged outsiders, mainly from the north, had moved into campus accommodation after paying large bribes to university officials.
Rubbish-strewn residences teemed with toddlers racing down corridors after women carrying buckets to bathrooms.
One man, who said he was from the south, lived in a room containing nothing but two cupboards. A large hole had been knocked through the wall to "enlarge" it with an adjacent room.
"I will not venture to say who was responsible for this. That would be mere speculation," said Llambi Stefanllari, a professor of forestry.
"Try to imagine how we feel. But we have to look forward. We opened our section back in 1959 with two chairs and nothing else. If we as academics aren't optimistic, who else will be?"
